title: Noida International Airport Opens for Commercial Flights June 15, Giving Delhi-NCR a Second Gateway
excerpt: India's largest greenfield airport at Jewar begins domestic operations with IndiGo, Akasa Air, and 140 weekly flights across 15 destinations
body:
# Noida International Airport Opens for Commercial Flights June 15, Giving Delhi-NCR a Second Gateway

## After years of delays, political wrangling, and a pandemic that froze construction timelines across India, the Noida International Airport at Jewar is finally set to welcome its first commercial passengers on June 15, 2026. The airport — coded DXN by IATA — will become the second international gateway for the sprawling Delhi–National Capital Region, complementing the perpetually congested Indira Gandhi International Airport.

IndiGo, India's largest carrier by market share, will operate the inaugural commercial flight: an 08:05 AM departure from Lucknow touching down at DXN on the morning of June 15. Budget carrier Akasa Air follows from June 16. Air India Express had been expected to join the launch roster but has postponed its DXN operations indefinitely, citing scheduling constraints.

## A Greenfield Behemoth

The airport was inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on March 28, 2026, after the Directorate General of Civil Aviation granted its aerodrome licence earlier that month. Built on a greenfield site in Gautam Buddha Nagar district of Uttar Pradesh, it is operated by Yamuna International Airport Private Limited, a subsidiary of Switzerland's Zurich Airport International AG, under a public-private partnership with the state government.

Phase I alone is impressive in scale: a single 3,900-metre runway capable of handling wide-body aircraft, 25 aircraft stands, nearly 50 check-in counters, and an initial passenger capacity of 12 million annually — roughly equivalent to Kolkata's Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose International Airport. The terminal can handle about 30 flights per hour and includes a multi-modal cargo hub with an initial capacity of approximately 2.5 lakh metric tonnes per year.

The launch schedule calls for 140 weekly flights connecting 15 domestic destinations, a number that airline executives say could grow rapidly once ground infrastructure is stress-tested through the monsoon season.

## Connectivity That Changes the Map

What makes DXN strategically significant is not just its capacity but its location. Situated along the Yamuna Expressway, the airport dramatically shortens travel times to Agra, Mathura, and the industrial corridors of western Uttar Pradesh. For travellers heading to the Taj Mahal, the drive from DXN is roughly 90 minutes — less than half the slog from IGI Airport through Delhi's notorious traffic.

Ground connectivity at launch includes bus services from Delhi, Uttarakhand, and Haryana. Mahindra has deployed a fleet of electric taxis at the terminal, and ride-hailing platforms Uber, Ola, and Rapido will all be operational from day one. A dedicated metro link is planned for later phases.

The airport's architecture draws from Indian heritage, with design elements inspired by ghats and havelis, blending cultural aesthetics with modern infrastructure. Sustainability is baked into the blueprint: the facility aims to achieve net-zero carbon emissions through energy-efficient systems and green building protocols.

## The Bigger Picture: India's Aviation Boom

DXN enters service at a moment when Indian aviation is straining at every seam. IGI Airport handled over 72 million passengers in 2025, pushing close to its operational ceiling. The government's UDAN regional connectivity scheme has expanded air travel to dozens of smaller cities, but hub airports have struggled to keep pace with demand.

The new airport is designed to scale. Future phases envision expansion to six runways and a capacity of 70 million passengers annually, which would make it one of the largest airports in the world. The total project cost for Phase I alone stood at ₹11,200 crore ($1.3 billion).

For the state of Uttar Pradesh, DXN represents a flagship infrastructure achievement. Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath has positioned the airport as an anchor for industrial development along the Yamuna Expressway corridor, with logistics parks, manufacturing zones, and a proposed Film City in the surrounding area.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the millions of Non-Resident Indians who travel to Delhi-NCR each year — whether for family visits, weddings, or business — a second airport is a material change in travel planning. IGI's Terminal 3, the primary international hub, is notorious for long immigration queues, baggage delays, and peak-season chaos. While DXN's international operations are still down the road, domestic connectivity from day one means NRIs landing at IGI can catch a quick domestic hop to DXN for onward travel to western UP, avoiding hours of road travel.

More importantly, when international flights do arrive at DXN — likely within the next two to three years as Phase II infrastructure comes online — diaspora travellers with roots in Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, and the Hindi heartland will have a direct gateway that bypasses Delhi entirely. This will not only enhance travel convenience but also strengthen family ties, as many NRIs frequently visit their ancestral homes.

Travel agents catering to the NRI market are already noting interest. "Anyone flying to Agra, Mathura, Aligarh, or even Lucknow now has to seriously consider DXN as their routing hub," said one Delhi-based travel consultant. "The expressway connectivity makes it a no-brainer once the flight network fills out."

Additionally, the airport's development is expected to boost remittances, as easier travel will encourage more NRIs to visit and invest in their home regions. This could lead to increased economic activity and job creation in Uttar Pradesh, benefiting both local communities and the diaspora.

## What Comes Next

The first weeks will be a proving ground. Airlines will watch load factors, ground handling teams will work out operational kinks, and passengers will render their verdict on everything from signage to security lines. The monsoon, arriving in earnest by late June, will test drainage systems and runway operations.

But the significance of the moment is hard to overstate. India now has a new major airport — its largest greenfield aviation project — and the Delhi-NCR region joins the ranks of global metropolises served by a true dual-airport system. For a country adding air passengers faster than almost any other on earth, DXN is not a luxury. It is a necessity whose time has come.
